blocks.text: Wild honey, flowing down from the clefts of rocks, was found in great quantity and tasted by STEPH. SCHULZ in the region where John the Baptist is said to have lived; see his travel account, which he entitled die Leitungen des Höchsten nach seinem Rathe auf den Reisen durch Europa, Asia und Africa, vol. 5, p. 133. The same is confirmed by Maundrell and Mariti, whose testimonies Oedmann has adduced in the Vermischten Sammlungen, fascicle 6, Chapter 20, p. 136 f.

Cf. TOURNEFORT, Voyage, vol. 3, p. 75. Learned men today report similar things of the honey collected in Georgia from the flowers of Azalea Pontica Linn. See the preface to the book IO. GEORG. MODELS kleine Schriften, St Petersburg, 1773, and BECKMANN on Aristotle, De auscultationibus mirabilibus, p. 45.

In this passage, however, Michaelis, in the Supplemm. vol. 2, p. 391 f., contends that honey made from raisins (on which see note 1 above) is to be understood. "Bees' honey," he says, "cannot possibly be meant. It would not only be a cheap gift, but all the more inept because it would be carrying owls to Athens; for Egypt abounds in honey, and indeed of the most excellent kind, having a spring and first harvest over two months. See Maillet's description of Egypt (description de l'Egypte, lettre neuvieme) p. 24, 25. Nor would anyone moderately acquainted with the nature of both regions think of palm honey; for Eretz Yisrael neither abounds in palms now nor ever greatly abounded in them, whereas Egypt is rich in them, and neighbouring Biledulgerid richer still, which even takes its name from the abundance of palms." Michaelis is followed by WARNEKROS in his treatise de fertilitate Palaestinae cum Aegypto comparata (in the Repertorio für bibl. und morgenl. Literat. vol. 15), §19, p. 221 ff. I doubt, however, whether in Jacob's time they knew how to boil syrup from raisins.

But PETR. ADRIAN. VAN KOOTEN, in Observatt. ad nonnulla Canticor. loca (under the presidency of SEBALDUS RAVIUS, Utrecht, 1774), p. 16 ff., refers that comparison used by the Hebrew poet not to pleasant speech but to the saliva of the beloved, which the later Oriental poets are accustomed to compare with honey. Thus NUWEIRI (in REISKE on Tarafa, last page), listing the flowers of the Arab poets which they use in praising their beloveds, mentions this one among others: شبهوا اللما بالخمر والريق بالشهد [shabbahū al-lamā bi-l-khamr wa-l-rīq bi-l-shahd] they compare the gum to wine, the saliva to honey. And MUTANABBI (in the Excerpts published by Reiske, p. 43, verse 7), describing his beloved, says: مظلومة القد في تشبيهه غصنا [maẓlūmat al-qadd fī tashbīhihi ghuṣnan] مظلومة الريق في تشبيهه ضربا [maẓlūmat al-rīq fī tashbīhihi ḍaraban] Her stature is wronged if it is compared to a branch; her saliva is wronged if it is compared to honey. So too IMRU' AL-QAIS, in the Poem adorned with the prize, edited by Lette, verse 15, addresses his beloved thus: فقلت لها سيري وارخي زمامه [fa-qultu lahā sīrī wa-arkhī zimāmahu] ولا تبعدني من جناك المعسل [wa-lā tubʿidīnī min janāki al-muʿassal] I said to her: let him (the camel) go with slackened rein, and do not keep me from your most honeyed fruit. By the most honeyed fruit he means her saliva, or kisses that equal honey in sweetness. TOGHRAI uses the same figure where, imagining himself pierced and nearly slain by the spears, that is, the eyes, of his beloved, he says (verse 25): يشفي لديغ العولي في بيوتهم [yashfī ladīgh al-ʿawlī fī buyūtihim] بنهلة من غدير الخمر والعسل [bi-nahlatin min ghadīr al-khamr wa-l-ʿasal] He who is wounded by spears will be healed in their tents by even a single draught from a pool of wine and honey. These passages moved Michaelis, in the Biblioth. Orient et Exeget. vol. 7, p. 169 ff., to think that in that passage of the Song lascivious kisses are meant, such as the Florentine kiss (a kiss given with the tongue inserted into the other's mouth and licking the tongue). But Velthusen, in his commentary on the passage, p. 364, contends that the common interpretation, which understands that passage of pleasant and sweet speech, is to be retained, chiefly because of the parallel passages IV, 3. V, 16. II, 3. Prov. V, 3.
Cicero, Divin. book 1. Val. Max. book 1, ch. 6. Aelian, Var. book 12, ch. 55.

I prefer, however, the conjecture of I. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. 2, p. 393, who compares the Arabic دَبْشٌ [dabshun], stripping off of the skin, so that the camel's hump would have been called דבשת from its chafing and ulceration.
